subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext:
What then is the necessity of Bill No. 19 which is at present on the order paper? If the government

Public Service-Salary Deduction
can act without legislative authority in deducting ten per cent of the salaries of civil servants, why go through the pretence of passing an act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext: I may say that the course pursued is not without precedent. I have reference particularly to a case as far back as 1S97, when the government of the day at that time withheld statutory increases without legislative authority and, I think, without sanction by order in council. But I must point out to my hon. friend that although I know technically parliament has not as yet passed the bill dealing with the deduction, there is the circumstance an interim supply bill was passed providing for only the amount less ten per cent.

subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext: The Interim Supply Bill was one for two months so that so far as it is concerned, there was no necessity for making the deduction. I appreciate the inconvenience that has been mentioned by my hon. friend and that might be occasioned by complying with the law, but the law is there and should be complied with. The position that we are in at the moment is that the government has assumed to act in the matter without any power from parliament. Bill No. 19, to provide for the deduction in compensation in the public service has received its second reading, but it is still in committee; it has not yet passed the Commons; it has not gone to the Senate and it has not received royal assent. My hon. friend knows that until a bill has passed both the Commons and the Senate and has received royal assent, it is not law and no action can be taken under it. This action has been taken without any legislative authority and it is simply substituting the directions of the ministry for the authority of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext: I must respectfully beg to differ from my right hon. friend. The governing factor is the voting of the money. Even if Bill No. 19 were passed, not a dollar could be paid to the servants of the crown unless and until the supply bill was passed, so that in the last analysis we must lean upon the Interim Supply Bill which takes distinct recognition of the fact we are proposing that salaries this year shall have a deduction of ten per cent.

subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES
speechtext: The governing factor is the authority of parliament and it has voted for the public service money amply sufficient for a complete payment of the civil service this month.

subtopic: TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM INDEMNITIES AND SAL.ARIES

speechtext: The fact that parliament voted an interim Supply bill in order to oblige the government is no reason why the latter should ignore parliament in the matter of following the procedure which is essential in all these affairs. I do not wish unduly to labour the point, but certainly one of the obligations devolving upon the leader of an opposition is to see that the rights of parliament in the matter of legislation are respected, and I cannot agree with my hon. friend as to there being any precedent which he could cite as authority for saying that the action which has been taken is legal. It is, I think, both arbitrary and illegal, and I repeat it is another instance of where the authority of parliament is superseded, not even by the sanction of the ministry as expressed in an order in council, but apparently by the will of the ministry as expressed in a mere verbal order.

I do not know that any
advantage will arise by an attempt on the part of my right hon. friend and myself to have the last word. Of course when the Interim Supply Bill was passed, my right hon. friend, as was quite right and proper, made the reservations usual in such cases. It was made very clear, and the record will show, that his having assented to the Interim Supply Bill does not commit him to the principle and leaves it open to him to discuss the estimates in full in precisely the same manner as if the Interim Supply Bill had never been passed. But I submit that the governing factor is the voting of the money and as I have said, the Interim Supply Bill gave specific recognition to the fact that the amount available covering the period of a year was to be made available to the extent of the ordinary sum for salaries, less the deduction of ten per cent. Under those circumstances I submit that not only is. the course we took proper and in conformity with the law, but it is the one that in the long run will cause least inconvenience to members of the public service.

The other evening when we
were discussing this item I asked the minister if he would tell the committee what was the policy of the government with reference to the shipment of grain through the port of Halifax. Another question I asked was, what quantity of grain had been shipped from the port of Halifax and the port of St. John in the last three years. This is a very important matter especially for the port of Halifax, in which of course I am more interested than in St. John, and I would like the minister to give the committee some statement in regard to that matter.

through the ports of Halifax and St. John for the last three years has been as follows:

I have not the figures under my hand of shipments through the ports of Montreal and Quebec. The question of the export of grain from the Atlantic ports in the winter concerns only the ports of Halifax and St. John after navigation has closed at Montreal. It must be borne in mind that the grain trade of Canada is carried on by private corporations, and once the grain is bought on the Winnipeg market, which, of course, is the large central market in this country dealing with grain, it passes into the hands of the owner who directs its movement as he considers to his own advantage. The movement of grain from Port Arthur and Fort William at the head of the lakes is to certain points in the east which best suit the purposes of the exporter. Some of the grain is moved to Buffalo, some to Port Colborne and other lake ports, or Montreal, as the case may be, and it is there held to the order of the owner. The owner may direct its export, in the case we will say of grain at Buffalo, either through American or Canadian ports at his own option, over which, of course, we exercise no authority or control. There are certain economic factors which enter in at the ports of Boston, New York and Portland, and at one or two other ports to a lesser degree. There is always a great deal of shipping offered with what is known as distress space, and frequently the owners of grain take advantage of the distress rates and contract for shipment through those ports; or it may be that the destination of the grain in Europe calls for shipment through ports other than Canadian, in the opinion of the owner of the grain. The movement of the grain is thus wholly in the control of the owner of the commodity. As far as the government is concerned, and I think what I say of the present government is true of preceding governments, all facilities possible for the handling of the grain have been provided in Canadian ports and will be provided as required in the future so far as possible. The influence of the government is used, so far as it is consistent with the movement of trade generally, in the direction of trade through Canadian channels. We have considered and will consider any suggestions which may be made which will facilitate the movement of grain in such channels. I would impress upon

the committee however that the grain is in the hands of the owners of the commodity who, naturally, direct its movement through such channels as they may consider desirable.
There is one other point to which I wish to draw the attention of hon. members. A great deal might be done to increase the movement of grain through Canadian channels if at the point of export or point of shipment there was a larger body of commercial interests connected with the movement of grain through that port. That is, if there were business concerns operating at these points, as there are at other older and more established points, who were interested in the movement or handling or direction of grain, the results would be more satisfactory. Only recently I drew the attention of business concerns in eastern Canada to the desirability of securing an increased interest on the part of Canadian business men concerning the movement of the Canadian crop, which forms such an important part of our export business.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with great interest to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Had I shut my eyes I should have thought I was back in the session of 1930; the then Minister of Trade and Commerce of that day was asked certain questions when complaints were made regarding this very question. I am sure the minister's man}' friends must have been delighted to hear him make the speech he has just made. I do not know however how some of my Conservative colleagues from the province of Nova Scotia took it, because they will remember that during the sessions of 1926, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the former government were bombarded -and properly so; I am not objecting at all

were properly bombarded by members representing constituencies in Nova Scotia who complained very bitterly that the government of my right hon. friend, the present leader of the opposition, had failed to see that grain went through the port of Halifax. In fact Conservative newspapers in the province of Nova Scotia referred to the elevator, which the late government had been instrumental in building, as a pigeon roost. The statement was made that very little if any grain was passing through the port, and of course the government of that day was blamed.
I noticed however the statement which the minister read with regard to the quantity of grain passing through the port of Halifax in the last two years, or since the present government took office. It would seem that since my friends from Nova Scotia have taken seats

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
on the government benches conditions are worse than they were when the late government- was in power. I need not go into this matter, but I may say that the minister's explanation, that to a great extent the matter is in the hands of the shipper, is quite right. I have always contended that, and there is no question about it. The fact is however that gentlemen who now are members of the government, or members supporting the government, told us two or three years ago that that was not correct, and that if they were put into power, if they were placed on the seats of the mighty, they would see that this condition was changed and that grain would flow through the ports of Halifax and St. John. There was no question about it. Not only in the newspapers but on the public platforms hon. gentlemen now sitting opposite made the distinct statement that the then Liberal government should be turned out of power and that the Conservative party should be given a chance to see that grain flowed more freely through the ports of Halifax and St. John. We wTere told of course that the Transcontinental railway was built for this special purpose, and the name of my late respected chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was brought into the discussion to show that when he and his government decided to build the Transcontinental railway the decision was made to fulfil the special purpose to which I am now referring. My hon. friends urged that the government led by the present leader of the opposition was not doing its duty by the people who had grain to ship, or to those people in the cities of St. John and Halifax, when they did not see that greater quantities of grain went through the ports of those two cities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, birds will come home to roost, even if they are pigeons sitting on the elevator at Halifax. I can understand why the Minister of Trade and Commerce hangs his head because, after sitting in this house from the years 1926 to 1930 and listening to his colleagues complain to the then government of what a terrible thing it was that these people of the maritime provinces were not receiving their maritime rights, he may well hang his head. We heard a great deal about one hundred per cent maritime rights. If the late government did not give one hundred per cent maritime rights, what has the present government done with regard to the shipment of grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John? The figures given by the minister only a few moments ago supply the answer, and in that connection I need not say very much more.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister must have thought the matter important when he made his speeches during the election campaign of 1930. Of course, perhaps he was not reported correctly. Sometimes we find, when we read extracts from speeches supposed to have been made by the right hon. gentleman, that they were not correct, because perchance, a mistake had been made by some cub reporter. I have before me however what the Prime Minister is reported to have said in the Forum at Halifax on July 3, 1930, just a few days before the election. At that time the people at Halifax were urged to turn the government out of office because of their treatment of the people of Nova Scotia with regard to the shipment of grain, and for other reasons. But they were told something further. At that meeting the Prime Minister made a distinct promise to the people of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces. What was he reported as saying? I quote as follows:
Speaking at the Forum at Halifax on July 3, 1930, Mr. Bennett said it was his "determination to force Canadian traffic over Canadian territory and through Canadian ports and to make this country commercially independent of the United States."
He was going to blast his way. I do not know whether he intended to blast the mountains through which the railway passed when coming from Winnipeg, but certainly he was going to do another blasting act so that grain might go through Canadian ports.
What has my right hon. friend done since he made that speech on July 3, 1930? Has he done anything for the ports of Halifax and St. John? I will come to that in a minute. Quoting again:
He said the development and equipment of the port of Halifax as a great national port was "essential to meet the competition from the United States ports of the Atlantic seaboard and to give maritime ports every advantage in low rates to attract traffic both inward and outward."
What has my right hon. friend or his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce done to obtain lower rates on grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John? During the last two years, what have they done? The minister gave us the answer only a few minutes ago; he told us of the infinitesimal quantity of grain which had passed through either the port of St. John or Halifax since hon. members opposite came into power. Quoting further:
He further declared that "his consideration was the welfare of Canada and Canadian ports -United States ports were not his concern; the people of that country were quite capable of looking after their own interest."



Supply-Trade-Grain Act
Yet, in spite of that statement-and no doubt that statement was made to get votes in the city of Halifax for my two hon. friends who represent that city-

And who are not in
the committee.

It does not matter. The fact
remains that the Prime Minister made that statement, I will not say deliberately, Mr. Chairman, because you might call me to order; but the Prime Minister, according to the newspapers, is reported to have said that if he and his government were elected he would see that grain would flow more freely through the port of Halifax, and, of course, through St. John. But since that date this government has done nothing. The minister himself admitted a moment ago that, unlike his leader, he was not concerned about freight going through the American ports; he said it was impossible to keep it from going through American channels. And he is quite right. But the Prime Minister did not give the electors of Halifax that understanding. He virtually said to them, "Elect me and my government and we will see to it that the elevators in Halifax and St. John will be full of wheat all the time; we will see that wheat will be flowing through these ports to foreign markets." Let us see whether they did anything else with regard to this great question.
In 1928 there was a meeting of the maritime board of trade at Moncton and I believe that at that meeting that board of trade, owing to the fact, I have no doubt, that they thought that the then government were not perhaps doing things as quickly as they should, and were not seeing that the maritime ports were being used properly, passed a resolution which reads:
1. That the National Transcontinental railway was constructed for the purpose of creating a route to Halifax and St. John that would provide for, among other matters, the transporting of Canada's exportable surplus of grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John at rates that would not exceed those to other
north Atlantic ports.
2.	That an all-rail rate of 19-34 cents per 100 pounds as requested in this application is necessary in order that the National Transcontinental railway be used for the purpose for which it was constructed.
3.	That the board did, in general order No.
448, dated August 26,	1927, recognize this
matter as one of national importance and directed the Canadian National Railways to publish an export rate, on grain, of 18-34 cents per 100 pounds to Quebec city. This order was complied with by the publication of C.N.R. tariff No. C.G. 93. G.R.C. No. E1268.
4.	That the same conditions and circumstances surround the extension of the export rate on

grain to St. John and Halifax as applied in the decision of the board with respect to the rate to Quebec city.
5.	That, in view- of the national importance of this matter, we would respectfully urge that it is expedient that this matter be given immediate attention by the board.
I am reading a resolution contained in a speech delivered Iby the hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) in the year 1928 when the late government was in power. I am not going to quote from the hon. gentleman's speech or recite his complaints with regard to the little -that had been done by the Liberal party. I do want however to back up what the hon. gentleman said on that occasion, because now his own government is in power. He has been supporting that government since 1930, nearly two years, and I have not heard either him or the senior member for Halifax say one word with regard to this very important matter.
Now the Liberal government did try to arrange this matter; they did endeavour to arrange for a differential rate of one cent per bushel. But they found, when they addressed themselves to the railway commission, that the commission indicated they could not do it unless legislation were enacted with respect to the question. The matter was referred to the government, and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has evidently forgotten the speech he made in the city of Halifax on July 3, 1930, inasmuch as he wanted to refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada. Instead of dealing with it as a government he wanted to pass the buck and refer the question to the courts. But now that this matter has again been referred to the government, the final arbiter, it has been or should have been before them for a number of months; and so far as the public and this parliament know, nothing has been done by the government to settle the question one way or the other, to see that a different rate is given whereby more grain can flow from the prairies through the ports of Halifax and St. John.
I say the government has been derelict in its duty in not settling this important question one way or the other, so that the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick may know exactly whether or not something is going to be done in their interests. All we have at the moment is the report of Sir Alexander Gibb. 1 dare say it was all right, and I am not complaining, to bring this eminent gentleman here to look into questions affecting the harbours of Canada; but I do say that Sir Alexander Gibb's report is not satisfactory to five per cent of the people of Canada interested in our different ports from Vancouver to Halifax.

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
Now what does Sir Alexander Gibb say about the port of Halifax? Surely the government might have given him some lead as they did when another commission sat in this country with respect to other matters. We remember that it was rumoured, when the Duncan commission was sitting, that the commission was given a hint that they were not to touch the tariff. Surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), if he is interested in his capacity of minister in charge of this deipartment, must have been taken into the confidence of Sir Alexander Gibb or taken him into his confidence. But if he was not taken into that gentleman's confidence it was the duty of the minister to see Sir Alexander before he made his report and give him his own views and ideas regarding this matter. What did Sir Alexander Gibb report so far as Halifax was concerned? He practically says that it is impossible to ship grain through the port of Halifax; it is even impossible, he says, to ship heavy freight through that port-and this notwithstanding the fact that the Conservative government in 1914 spent $35,000,000 on that port, and the fact that during the last seven and eight years, and especially during the time that the Liberal party was in power, other millions were spent developing the port of Halifax. Yet Sir Alexander Gibb now comes along and declares that it is impossible to ship heavy freight through that port. All that the people of Halifax and Nova Scotia can expect from his report is to have a few passengers land at that port from time to time.
1 say that the government should come to a decision promptly with regard to this question. Let the people of Halifax and Nova Scotia know what is going to be done. Let the citizens of Canada, who have spent tens of millions of dollars developing the port and getting it ready for the grain trade and other heavy traffic, know whether Sir Alexander Gibb's recommendation will be accepted, or whether the government will find means to send grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John.

I wish to say a few words
on the subject that has been discussed by my hon. friend (Mr. Duff). I have not the documents before me, but my recollection is that a very important decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners was given on October 28, 1930. An application had been made by the Halifax harbour commission and the transportation committee of the maritime board of trade for a one cent differential, so-called, over the Quebec rate. That means this. There was, prior to 1927, a rate from the 41761-129J
head of the lakes ports to the city of Quebec of 34-5 cents per hundred pounds, and a rate to the maritime ports of 35-5 per hundred pounds, one cent higher. Now certain interests in the city of Quebec, or the city, applied to the Board of Railway Commissioners and had the 34-5 rate reduced to a rate of 18-34. Thereupon an application was made by the bodies I have mentioned-that is, the Halifax harbour commission and the transportation committee of the maritime board of trade-for a rate from the head of the lakes ports to maritime ports of 19 - 34 cents per hundred pounds, preserving the one cent differential. The Board of Railway Commissioners decided against the applicants. I believe their decision was given about October 28, 1930. Some months later a petition was lodged with the governor in council requesting a variation or rescission of the decision of the board, under the section of the act which enables such action to be taken by the governor in council. That letter was dated December 10, 1931. It is a little too long to read in full, otherwise I should like to place it on Hansard. It states that this matter is of vital and urgent concern to these communities and to the province of Nova Scotia as a whole. The letter states:
One of the most immediate needs of the port of Halifax, and the channels of transportation of which it is the terminus, is a fair share of the movement of the Canadian grain crop. This need is twofold:
1.	To increase the volume of traffic through the port; and
2.	To provide the port with an adequate amount of grain for use as ballast cargo.
Then follow a number of very striking facts showing the large proportion of Canadian grain going through United States ports. Then the letter goes on to discuss the Quebec rate, which I have already mentioned. It says:

To Quebec	 34-5

Quebec applied for and secured a reduction of this rate to 18-34 cents per 100 pounds. And in its general order No. 448 the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada directed the railway to publish this reduced rate over the Transcontinental to the port of Quebec.
On two occasions the railways attempted to upset this rate, once before the board of railway commissioners, and again before the Supreme Court of Canada. Both attempts were unsuccessful. The application of the C.N.R. for leave to appeal from the judgment of the board was dismissed by that body in July, 1929; and in the Supreme Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Lamont, shortly after that date, also dismissed an application of the C.N.R. for leave to appeal from general order 448.
Meanwhile, an application had been made to the board of railway commissioners for an extension of the "Quebec rate" (plus the usual 1 cent differential) to the ports of Halifax and Saint John. This application, and the facts supporting it, were in every particular similar to the application and the facts pertaining to the Transcontinental railway in its relation to the port of Quebec, but certain members of the railway board, having granted the Quebec

application, reversed their position and denied the maritime application. The result is that the rate on grain and grain products over the Transcontinental from the bead of the lakes to maritime ports is approximately twice the rate to the port of Quebec.
The bodies making the unsuccessful application-the Halifax Harbour Commission and the Transportation commission of the Maritime Board of Trade-are carrying this case on appeal to your government, in the confident hope of securing a reversal of such an unjust and discriminatory action.
The port of Halifax is equipped immediately to handle twenty millions of bushels of grain during the shipping season. Established at this port is a modern elevator with a storage capacity of 2.200,000 bushels, but this elevator lies idle so far as the Canadian export grain traffic is concerned, and little or no Canadian grain comes over the railway lines into and through this province.
It is unnecessary here to attempt an _ enumeration of the benefits, direct and indirect, that would be derived by our own people from a substantial share of the grain traffic of the country. At this time, when unemployment is such a serious problem, the provision of more jobs for workers on our railways, in our mines and along our waterfront, to say nothing of the stimulation of other forms of industrial and commercial activity, would justify an unusual effort to hold the trade of Canada in Canadian channels.
The chairman of the Halifax Harbour Commission has stated his belief that the port of Halifax has just about reached the limit of its development unless an adequate share of the Canadian grain traffic can be secured, for, manifestly, it is going to be difficult, if not impossible, to develop any turn-around movement of liner tonnage under existing conditions.
In these circumstances, so vital not to this port and province alone, but to the dominion, as a national matter, we respectfully urge an early hearing of the appeal in the Transcontinental grain rates case, _ and a favourable decision in the interests of our own transportation channels. We realize the heavy burdens and great complexities involved in public administration in this country to-day. but we are confident that, appreciating the urgency of this matter from the standpoint of our national well-being, you and your government will give it early and effective attention.
Yours respectfully,
Then follow the signatures of the gentlemen I have named. After that letter was written the appeal did come on for hearing before the government, according to newspaper despatches, but so far as I have been able to learn as yet it has not been disposed of.
I submit to the minister that there can be no justification for these almost interminable delays in dealing with a comparatively simple matter. First we had the delay from last spring until January before the appeal came on for hearing at all, and we have had the delay month by month ever since. The question of the principles that should guide the government in dealing with these appeals was

up for discussion in committee of the whole two or three times last year. It has been laid down, and I do not think it can be denied, that the government are not acting as a court and are not setting precedents that can be applied to other cases. They are not bound by the ordinary rate-making principles which bind the Board of Railway Commissioners. The very object of the section is to enable them to put policies into effect, and the policy of the government as announced before the election was to stimulate the flow of grain through Halifax.
The promises .made by the Prime Minister have been read by my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough. Why does not the government act in the matter? That is the question I should like to direct to some responsible minister of the crown. If they have decided in their own minds not to give effect to the appeal why do they not courageously say so? Mr. Chairman, I think the committee, particularly those members from the maritime provinces, welcome the statement of the minister that this matter is under consideration, but I, for one, am filled with a great deal of apprehension at the rather ominous suggestion made that perhaps we would prefer to have delay in this matter rather than to have the door slammed at once in our face.
I was referring to the one point, namely, that an immediate decision should be given in connection with the appeal made by the hon. member.

That is the point with which I am dealing. After the strong appeals made by the hon. members for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) and Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), I hesitate to press this matter any further, but in the hope that something

I may say may have some influence upon the minister, I desire to say a word or two on the subject.
The minister says that this matter is not simple, but to my mind the only element of complication is the argument which has been made quite frequently to the effect that it will in some way cause a reduction in the tariffs of the American roads and thus lead to no practical effect. That is perhaps the strongest argument or is at least the statement most frequently made in opposing this rate. The Board of Railway Commissioners reduced the rate per hundred pounds on wheat moving from Port Arthur, Fort William, West Fort William and Armstrong to Quebec from 344 cents to 18-34 cents per hundred pounds. This action was taken regardless of possible clashes with American roads, and the order was issued on August 26, 1927. I had the honour to represent the maritime board before the railway commission, on first general freight rate hearing, and I supported the application then made by Quebec but asked that the same rate be extended to Halifax and St. John with the addition of a one cent differential. Before any decision was given the Duncan commission intervened and as a result of its finding the Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed. That disposed of most of the matters in the general freight rates investigation. The grain rates were subsequently discussed again before the Board of Railway Commissioners. I was not representing the maritimes on that hearing as I had become a member of the government. The order w'as granted for Quebec but no order was made so far as Halifax and St. John were concerned. I would point out to the committee that at the time of the application to the board, there was in existence a grain rate from these western points of Port Arthur, Fort William, West Fort William and Armstrong to Quebec which was just one cent less than the grain rate to St. John and Halifax; in other words, there was a differential of one cent in the rates to these ports. I cannot see any complication in this matter. All that the maritime provinces are asking for is a continuance of this differential of one cent between the Quebec rate and the St. John and Halifax rate.
Under the terms of the order Quebec now has a rate of 18-34 cents per hundred pounds, and unless an adjustment is made it will mean that Quebec will have a rate of 18-34 cents as compared with the rate of 354 cents to Halifax and St. John whereas the previous rates were 344 cents to Quebec and 354 cents to St. John and Halifax.
Quebec is not a winter port.

The Halifax harbour
commissioners in June, 1928. applied to the Board of Railway Commissioners to reopen the matter and grant the lower rate to Halifax and St. John to correspond with the new Quebec rate and the maritime board of trade joined them. There should be no complication in deciding that the old differential should apply; if the rate has been reduced to Quebec, then it should be reduced correspondingly to St. John and Halifax. This is all the complication there is and it is all the government has to determine. I desire to compliment both the old Halifax harbour commission and the new commission and the maritime board of trade on the excellent way in which this case has been presented, both to the Board of Railway Commissioners and to the governor in council. Therefore I come back again to ask my hon. friend with his colleagues to consider favourably the application on appeal which has been made from the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners and to give a prompt decision allowing that application.

My doubt is due to this fact: a large proportion of the grain that is shipped through the port of New York is carried -by the large liners. Why is that so? Simply because those large transatlantic boats, coming in and sailing as they have to do, on schedule time, must, due to their great superstructures, be given considerable quantities of dead-weight ballast and the most convenient type of dead-weight cargo they can obtain is grain. In former years, when the United States were shipping considerable quantities of lead, copper and other heavy commodities of that kind, those liners were able to obtain, to some extent, at all events, the dead-weight ballast which they required. Under present conditions that class of commodity is not available. Those vessels, depending on their size, must get the stiffening they require, representing 3,000, 5,000, 8.000 tons on each eastern voyage. I have known liners actually to pay as much as one cent a bushel for tlje privilege of carrying grain from New York to Europe and tens of thousands of bushels of grain have been carried at from one-half to two or three cents a bushel. That is a condition of affairs that no adjustment of railway rates in Canada can obviate. There is one way in which the situation can be met, and if our hon. friends opposite are prepared to take that step I should be glad to know they have the courage to take it, and that is to prohibit the export of grain through any other than Canadian national ports. If they are prepared to do that, the grain of the western provinces will go through the ports of Halifax and St. John during the winter and through Montreal in the summer. But apart from that I am afraid no very large proportion of grain from the western provinces will be taken away from United States Atlantic ports, particularly New York, as long as modern great Atlantic liners must have a large amount of dead-weight ballast, and with say eight or ten big liners sailing eastwardly weekly, each carrying from one hundred and fifty to four hundred thousand bushels of

I well remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if I am not mistaken, preaching a sermon to us when we sat to the right of the Speaker, about encouraging Canadian ports. Let me give a little matter of history. In 1928-29, the rate from the head of the lakes to Quebec was 34 cents, and to St. John and Halifax 35 cents and a fraction, but let us deal with round figures. What do we find? The port of St. John handled 27,000,000 bushels of grain, and when we were handling 27,000,000 bushels of grain in St. John we were told that there was too much Canadian grain going through American ports, and that that was our fault. The rate from the head of the lakes to Quebec was 34 cents, and the rate from the head of the lakes to the maritime ports, 35 cents.

Quebec got a reduction from 34 cents to 18 cents, and when we in the maritimes pleaded for a rate on a basis of the rate that we had before, when the Quebec rate was 34 cents, I will not say we were refused it by the railway commission, but when the Quebec case was placed before the railway commission the case of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, or the St. John and Halifax case, was not presented in the same light as the Quebec case. A gentleman by the name of Mr. Duchemin, a lawyer from Sydney, I think, represented the Nova Scotia government at that time before the railway commission, looking on only. His statement before the railway commission at that time was: I am representing the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but I am not here at the present moment to push their claims. I do agree, he said, with the arguments of the city of Quebec, and I hope that the commission will see their way clear to grant the request of the city of Quebec for a reduction in the rate. Later on, when some of the commissioners drew his attention to the fact that they were convinced that the claims of St. John and Halifax were properly before the board, Mr. Duchemin stated to the commission before that sitting adjourned, that on the request of his superiors he was withdrawing the Nova Scotia and New Brunswick claims-
Pardon me, that is not what he said.

Now what happened? Mr. Chairman, as a former minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce and as a member in the committee representing a province which is not as vitally interested in the movement of grain through the maritime ports as are the hon. members representing western Canada and the province of Nova Scotia, I should like to say a word or two in support of the minister's position concerning endeavours made towards the movement of grain through the maritime ports.
To the present Minister of Trade and Commerce I should say that I believe the department under his administration is just as anxious as it was when I had the honour to hold his position, to ship as much of our grain as we possibly can through Canadian ports. The late government did provide the facilities. There is now an opportunity, by governmental action to provide a rate which will demonstrate whether or not grain can be handled in any substantial quantity through these ports. In other words, if the present government grants the request of my hon. friends from this side of the house my hon. friends opposite and the senators, I do not think that at the moment much more can be done except to encourage shippers to prove whether or not we can export a substantial quantity of grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John.
There is much truth in the statements of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and in those of the minister. We in this parliament however must remember that sometimes we can be a bit too selfish in our national viewpoints. We can be too selfish in our national viewpoint with regard to trade

as we can with regard to tariffs; sometimes these things are two-edged swords. I think the minister will agree that the figures have not changed very much and that we enjoy through the port of Montreal about the same export of American grain as the United States enjoys of Canadian grain through the port of Buffalo. Through the years there has been a fairly even balance, and no doubt my western friends realize that some of the export of American grain through the port of Montreal has, in the past, been very helpful to them. Especially is that true concerning certain lower grades of Canadian barley. A market has been found for that barley, whether high or low grade, by mixing in the port of Montreal with American barley, making an admixture more suitable to the continental trade. Likewise we must remember-and this is not a selfish recommendation favouring the west-[DOT] that the Canadian ports enjoy a very substantial import trade destined for the United States. Especially does that apply on the Pacific seaboard. So, I say, if the facilities and the . rate structure which I know the minister is anxious to give, can induce a greater trade through our maritime ports, I believe every hon. member in the house is prepared to support the granting of the rate. As the hon. member for Pictou has said, complete control of movement through maritime ports can be brought about by putting into effect very drastic * regulations,-regulations which I believe every hon. member must realize might lead to retaliation which would be more disastrous in its effect than the regulations would be beneficial. Therefore I say to my hon. friends from the maritime provinces that as a former minister I thoroughly support them in their request for a one cent differential and I support the minister in his endeavours to increase. trade through these ports iby inducing shippers to make greater use of the facilities provided.
The ports of Halifax and St. John simply must be maintained as they are Canada's only winter Atlantic outlets. There is no politics in connection with this matter. In the past, as in the present, this house has been prepared to sustain and support any rate structure which will enable us to bring as much of our western grain as possible through Atlantic ports. I do not however think we would be adopting the wise course if we were to force upon the minister regulations or suggestions which in the aggregate or in the long run might react unfavourably on his department in other ways. I believe the rate structure or differential asked for by my hon. friends has the minister's sympathetic consideration. He

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
fully realizes the tremendous investment which has been made by past governments in harbour facilities; he realizes the investments made in elevator facilities. I am quite satisfied the minister will do everything in his power to facilitate the movement of grain through the Atlantic ports.

Mr. Chairman, I am very
sorry I was not in my place when this item was first brought to the attention of the committee. I was quite surprised to learn of the show staged here this afternoon by Nova Scotia and New Brunswick members, with only one exception. It is not very difficult to find a reason for it. If we look at the Halifax Herald of Thursday, April 14, yesterday, we see on the front page, in large letters, the following:
Prime Minister urged to act on maritime appeal. Senators and members declare N.T.R. grain rates case should not be referred back to any body that has already dealt with question.
Now I can understand the panic. Now I can easily understand why the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) gets up in his place and expresses his solicitude for the port of Halifax. Now I can understand why the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) becomes so suddenly alarmed because the port of Halifax is not getting sufficient business. Now I can also understand the attitude of the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) and the attitude of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Aeniot). The member for Gloucester wondered why, when this petition was being drawn up, the cooperation of the Liberal members was not asked. Well, there was a debate here for some three or four weeks and the cooperation of the opposition members was asked to facilitate the passing of the unemployment relief bill, but there was very little cooperation from that side. "We will give you cooperation if you will give us our pound of flesh"; that was the cooperation we got from hon. gentlemen opposite. It is no wonder that these hon. gentlemen become so suddenly interested in the matter under discussion. I am told the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough quoted from a speech I made in this house.
No; I did not quote your speech at all. I said you made a speech.

Very well; the hon. member referred at any rate to a speech I made in 1926. I well remember it. The hon. gentleman asked whether I was as much interested now as I -was then. I am just as much interested, and more so. But, sir, I am not going
to use every opportunity to stand up in this house and bring to the attention of parliament, either in the house or in this committee, what my attitude is and what my demands are with regard to the port of Halifax. I am making my representations in what I consider the proper way. I am not looking for cheap newspaper advertising or notoriety.
What about the Mc-Conachie family?

I did not bring to the attention of the house the McConachie case for any advertising. If hon. gentlemen will read Hansard they will find that when I made my address on behalf of that family I made it quite plain that I had been asked to do so by a chaplain at the port of Halifax. And that gentleman was not of my political stripe. He was and is a member of one of the outstanding Liberal families of Quebec. I deny what the hon. member for North Temiskaming says, when he charges that I was looking for notoriety or playing politics in that regard.
We remember it.

You can remember it if
you wish to. I would remind hon. gentlemen that for nine years, they sat here as supporters of a government, of the same party which introduced the National Transcontinental bill into this parliament in 1903. I quoted in my address in this house in 1926 some of the statements of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the promises of the Liberal party with regard to forcing the trade of Canada east and west, and in looking through an editorial in the same paper to which I have already referred I find that on July 30, 1903, the then Prime Minister of Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in asking for leave to introduce a bill to provide for the construction of a National Transcontinental railway, said in the course of his speech on that occasion:
Let me observe that if we have used American ports, it is not because of five months in the year our own ports are icebound . . . but simply because we had no railways to reach them. In the face of this, are the Canadian parliament and people going to stand on their manhood and place us in such a position that at aill times of the year, not only by one railway, but by two or more, we shall have access from January to December to our own harbours, and be able to say to our American neighbours: "Take off your bonding privilege whenever it suits you, we are commercially independent."
In the same address the right hon. gentleman went on:
The Canadian confederation would have been a union on paper and a union on paper only, but for the fact that the Grand Trunk railway, and the Canadian Pacific railway and the
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

Intercolonial railway brought all parts of our country together to act in unison and to beat with the same heart. This new railway will be another link in that chain of union. It will not only open territory hitherto idle and unprofitable; it will not only force Canadian trade into Canadian channels; it will not only promote citizenship between old Canada and new Canada, but it will secure us our commercial independence, and it will forever make us free from the bondage of the bonding privilege. For that reason alone, in my estimation, it would be worth all the sacrifices and far more than we are called upon to make.
I ask this committee: What did Sir Wilfrid Laurier mean by that, if he did not mean that it was his intention and the intention of his government to force Canadian goods through Canadian channels and have them shipped through Canadian ports? I ask further:	Was that the attitude of hon. members opposite during the nine years from 1921 to 1930? They had before them the words of their leader, the greatest Liberal leader Canada has ever had. They knew what he had said when he introduced this bill, namely, that he intended to force Canadian trade through Canadian ports. Hon. gentlemen opposite had their opportunity, but they lay down on the job.
Oh, oh.

You can laugh if you like. You laugh at every sensible observation made on this side of the house. I see my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), that brilliant gentleman, the only man in God's world who knew that Britain was going off the gold standard. If ever this house had occasion to laugh, it was when that gentleman told the house he knew all about Britain's intention to go off the gold standard.
I think he might be quiet for a little while.
I do not engage the attention of this house on many occasions, and I do not intend to fill up the pages of Hansard now. I simply rose to tell hon. gentlemen on the other side just where I stand with regard to the development of the port of Halifax and the trade to that port. I stand, as I always have stood, ready and willing to do my part on all occasions to impress upon this government or upon any other government the importance of shipping the products of this country through the ports of Halifax and St. John.
Where would this country have been from 1914 to 1918 if, during five months of the year, we could not have sent Canadian troops and materials to the war area from the ports of St. John and Halifax? The majority of our soldiers were sent from Halifax, as well as a great many American troops, and a great many of these soldiers came back through

the same port. That illustrates the importance of developing those ports and keeping them in proper condition, and I say again to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his colleagues that we in Nova Scotia look to this government for every assistance it can possibly give in the development of our port, and I feel quite certain that as soon as the opportunity presents itself they will give us that assistance for which we have petitioned on many occasions.

I think it is to be regretted that after I and other Nova Scotia and New Brunswick members have risen in our places this afternoon in order to impress upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce the importance of using the great ports of Halifax and St. John, the junior member for Halifax should refer to our remarks as a show. It may be a show for him; he reminds me of the story I read, when a boy, of Rip Van Winkle, who slept for twenty years.
Mr. QUINN; You slept for nine years.

My hon. friend has been sleeping in this parliament, as far as the shipment of grain through Halifax is concerned, for the last three sessions, and he should foe the last member to refer to our discussion this afternoon as a show, especially when I, who do not represent the port of Halifax, come to his help in trying to get more business for that port.
A political show.

My hon. friend also tries to make out that I would not have risen in mv place in connection with this matter if it had not been for the fact that the Nova Scotia members supporting the government discussed this question with the government during the last few days. I am very glad that they did so, but my hon. friend is not fair nor is he correct. Evidently he was out of the house when the discussion started this afternoon, and he .must have been out of the house a week ago to-night as well, when I asked the minister to tell us the policy of the government with regard to the shipment grain through the port of Halifax. I might say to my hon. friend that in my opinion the reason for the meeting of the Nova Scotia members with the government during the last three or four days was that the hon. member for Gloucester and myself rose in our places last Friday night to ask what was the policy of the government. Evidently we must have awakened the Rip Van Winkle from Halifax.
My hon. friend also says that we are trying to get some cheap political notoriety

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
out of this discussion. I wonder what the people of Halifax will think of that statement when they read that my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, my hon. friend from Hants-Kings, my hon. friend from Gloucester and myself endeavoured to induce the minister to do something for these two great ports. I am sure they will not call it cheap newspaper advertising. The only reference I made to my hon. friends from Nova Scotia was this: I said that during the years the Liberal party was in power some of my hon. friends from Nova Scotia upbraided the government day in and day out for not doing as much as they thought should be done to have grain shipped through the port of Halifax. I wanted to show the minister that my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax, who was so insistent at that time in asking why grain was not going through that port, has been very silent for the two years this government has been in office, though we find that to-day less grain is going through the port of Halifax than went through it when the Liberal government was in power. It is all very well for my hon. friend to lay a bouquet on the tomb of the great chieftain of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with regard to the Transcontinental railway. First my hon. friend says the Liberal party did nothing to ship grain through Halifax, and in almost the next breath he gives credit to Sir Wilfrid Laurier for building the Transcontinental in order that grain might flow through the ports of St. John and Halifax.
What did my hon. friend and his friends do with regard to the Transcontinental railway after the Liberal government was defeated in 1911? That road was built by the Liberal party, who went to the country in 1904 on that issue. I do not know what position my hon. friend took then, in his younger days, but we do know what was done by the Tory party, and we do know their attitude in 1904 with regard to the construction of that railway. They opposed it to the very limit; they did not say one word in favour of it, but my hon. friend says now that while Sir Wilfrid Laurier should get great credit for the construction of that line, the Liberals should be condemned because they did not use the road during the nine years they were in power. Does not my hon. friend know the reason why that road was not used during those nine years, or for that matter during the last twenty years? It was because the ministry of Sir Robert Borden was hardly sworn in before it degraded the Transcontinental railway. It is a well known fact that the road was not finished when the Liberal party was defeated, and what was
done by our Conservative friends from Nova Scotia, and for that matter from every part of the country, with regard to that great enterprise? They deliberately increased the grades and put wooden bridges where it had been intended to use iron bridges. That was one reason why the road was not used; the grades were so heavy that the engines could not pull enough cars to make it profitable to ship grain over that line from Quebec to Moncton.
You had better shade that a little.
It is true that the grades were made steeper than they were supposed to be. I do not know the technical term; perhaps the Minister of Railways could tell me, but there is no question about it.
You are off the track a little.

No, I am not. I know I am making my hon. friend from Pictou squirm in his seat, but I cannot help it. So I say it does not lie in the mouths of my hon. friends opposite to make out that in their nine years in power the Liberal party did nothing in order to encourage the shipment of grain through the ports of Halifax and St. John. Will not my hon. friend admit that the Liberal party did try to do something? Who built the elevator in Halifax? Was that done by the Conservative party? It is quite true that when the elevator was being built, and when the Liberal government and the harbour commission were endeavouring to do something so that grain would pass through the port of Halifax, the newspaper from which my hon. friend just read said it was useless to build that elevator, that the pigeons would roost on it and no grain would pass through it. If I am not mistaken my hon. friend either used those words himself or said, "Amen" when the Halifax Herald used them. So it does not lie in the mouth of my hon. friend now to say that we on this side are rising in our places this afternoon only because we were forced to do so by a meeting of Conservative members which took place several days after my hon. friend from Gloucester and I brought up this question in the house. Both my hon. friend from Gloucester and I are delighted to have the support of the Conservative members from the province of Nova Scotia, all I can say is: More power to their elbows, and may their efforts be crowned with success. If the government is to do anything I know it will not be done because of what has been said by the hon. member for Gloucester and

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
myself; my hon. friends will try to take the credit 'and I, for one, am willing to give it to them. If the government will put a one cent differential into effect as between Quebec and Halifax and St. John, then I am sure that both the hon. member for Gloucester and I will be very pleased. We will be only too glad to see the port of Halifax obtain a greater amount of business.
My non. friend did not say what he thought about Sir Alexander Gibb's report, and I wonder if he has taken that up with the government. Is he going to be satisfied that no heavy freight shall go through the port of Halifax? The Conservative party has spent, or perhaps I should say wasted, $35,000,000 on this port because the terminal should never have been built at its present location. One-third or one-quarter of that amount would have been sufficient to construct the terminal in the northern part of the harbour and better facilities would have been provided. The fact remains that $35,000,000 was spent by the Conservative party after it came into power in 1911, and the Liberal party has spent more money on this port than it was justified in spending. Money was spent on Halifax which should have been distributed throughout the province, and yet my hon. friend gets up and says that in nine years the Liberal party did nothing for the port of Halifax. During the Liberal regime millions of dollars were spent in providing new facilities in order to encourage freight and passenger traffic through that port. I and other hon. members on this side from Nova Scotia will do everything in our power, whether in opposition or supporting the government, to see that all possible business goes through this great port on the Atlantic ocean.

Mr. Chairman, I trust I may be pardoned for delaying the committee while I make a few observations on this important question. This is too vital a matter to be the subject of partisan bickerings. To my mind the policy of the routing of Canadian grain through American ports almost challenges the competency of this country as to the utilization of a great Canadian railway, the Transcontinental, built for a specific purpose and at tremendous cost- I understand upwards of $300,000,000. I have not the figures before me, but as I recollect, in 1931, five times as much Canadian grain was routed through the American Atlantic seaports as passed through the Canadian Atlantic seaports. Canadian grain is being routed through American ports in such huge volume as to build up a business in the

United States estimated in 1931, as being worth $20,000,000 to that country. This was the amount of Canadian money expended in the United States to cover the movement and other costs of Canadian grain over American lines and through American ports, while our own ports at Halifax and St. John were being starved for business. During an eight-year period from 1924 to 1931 inclusive, a total of 841,801.868 bushels of Canadian grain passed through American Atlantic seaports, while during the same eight-year period those same American ports handled but 296,025,798 bushels of American grain, nearly four times as much.
The question of the building of the National Transcontinental Railway has been discussed before in this house, and the pronouncements which were made in parliament and during the elections of 1904 and 1908 have been made and do not need to be repeated. The Gibb report is very disappointing so far as Halifax is concerned, inasmuch as it intimates that this port cannot look to the future with any degree of hope for the expansion of heavy basic cargoes, that it must depend principally on package freight. Those familiar with transportation matters and questions of shipping tell me that package freight invariably follows the basic cargo, so if we are unable to obtain the basic cargo-and practically the only basic cargo in this country is grain-then we have little or no chance of securing the package freight. In that respect, and in respect to many other angles to which I shall not refer, the Gibb report is very discouraging.
The former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) has said that this is a serious problem, and with that we all agree. The hon. member also stated that we might lay ourselves open to some measure of retaliation if we embraced too strongly any direct action with respect to the routing of Canadian grain entirely through Canadian ports. As I said before, in 1931, four times as much Canadian grain was shipped through American ports as American grain through Canadian ports, so the question of retaliation is not at all serious so far as we are concerned.

In referring to Canadian
Atlantic ports, does the hon. member include Montreal?

Yes, Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, but I excluded the Pacific ports. As I said, this matter is one which challenges our competency to deal effectively with the routing of Canadian trade over Canadian steel and through Canadian ports. I am sure every effort will be made to see that this wrong is rectified and that

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
there shall be a complete utilization of our Canadian ports, and particularly the ones in which I am most interested, the ports of Halifax and St. John.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to have some information from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in connection with the elevator at Prince Rupert which was built in 1926. Immediately after it was opened, it was leased to the Alberta wheat pool. During 1926 and 1927, several million bushels of grain went through that elevator; in 1928 and 1929 about the same amount; in 1930 and 1931 there was one cargo and in 1932 there has been no cargo so far. I ask this question because I understand the lease will expire within a short time. Does the government intend to re-lease it to the Alberta wheat pool which uses it only as a storehouse? Will the minister enlighten me on that subject?

This elevator is leased to the Alberta pool, and I do not know of any other body of exporters that are more efficient in the handling of their export business than are the pool operators of the prairie provinces. They are now divided into three pools, but sometimes the three operate under one sales agency. They now operate their own sales business, which is efficiently handled and which is in charge of the export trade. At the present time this elevator is full of grain -not moving, I admit-owned by the pool. The movement of grain through Prince Rupert depends naturally on the condition of shipping and the markets, chiefly of the orient. Unfortunately for Prince Rupert-I suppose I can only put it in that way-the main shipping on the Pacific coast calls at Vancouver. Through that port, if I recollect rightly, the export of grain is much larger than it was last year and has reached around 65,000,000 bushels; the movement is free and very large. There is nothing the government has done or can do that will move that grain through Prince Rupert if the owners of the grain do not find the facilities there for its movement to be an advantage over or on a par with those of other ports. As I said a moment ago with regard to the other matter, the grain is in the hands of its owners and they direct its movements. The lease is a very moderate one; the rate is low; the freight rates are low; everything that the country can do has been done for the movement of shipments through that port. The lease, I may say, expires next year. When the time comes the government will consider what is the best thing to do, whether to renew the lease if it is so desired,
or to make a new lease with other parties; but that point has not yet been under consideration.
Have the Alberta wheat pool applied for a renewal of the lease?
Not yet.

As a member representing a New Brunswick constituency, I do not think I should let this occasion pass without making some brief observations. I should like to preface my remarks with the statement that I enter into this discussion in no controversial spirit. As has been well said by my colleague from the county of Cumberland, to us in the maritime provinces, especially those of us who are interested in the great national ports of St. John and Halifax, this whole question transcends partisanship. I should like the house to visualize the entire question in that spirit.
Ever since the days of the decline of wooden shipping in the maritime provinces, our people have visualized the utilization of those two national ports as the winter ports of Canada. I am not very old, but my mind goes back to the year 1895, when the Beaver line first used St. John as a winter port. Prior to that time shipments of Canadian products across the ocean had been through Portland. Boston or other United States ports. The citizens of St. John put up a strong battle to controvert the idea that our ports were not usable during the winter season. It was the old government of which Sir George Foster was Minister of Finance that granted the first subsidy for the shipment of goods through Canadian ports including St. John. That was but the beginning, and from that time on the citizens of St, John expended their money and credit in an effort to build up a winter port.
The battle, however, has been a long one, and their hopes have been deferred. It is time that parliament, with the cooperation of every shade of public opinion in the house, dealt with this problem.
I listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and am appreciative of the fact there are great difficulties in the way. But I should like to impress upon him and hon. members generally that while his statement that the routing of grain is in the hands of the owner is primarily correct; yet grain shipments will travel along the lines of least resistance, and the most important factor is the question of rates. That, I think, is a fundamental principle, and it is only by a reduction in the grain rates that we can, by the natural evolution of business, have that

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
traffic routed through our own ports. Frankly I have always recognized that geography is against the principle for which we are contending; we cannot shut our eyes to the fact; but because of that, we have to take other measures and we ask the cooperation of western shippers to that end. Surely the maritime provinces have done their share in building up the west; surely we have contributed our resources to the building of the railways there, and we ask the western people who are shipping grain to recognize that fact and to reciprocate in some degree. I am not complaining that the shippers utilize the cheapest routes, but I know of no other way whereby this difficulty can 'be overcome and the hopes and aspirations of our citizenship in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick realized, than by making the freight rates attractive. Therefore I urge that steps be taken to put St. John and Halifax rates on a parity with Quebec rates, so-called, plus the differential of one cent. Let us try that out.
I am sorry there has been interjected into this debate this afternoon an element of partisanship. I suppose that is natural in a house composed of two major political parties, but I should like to remind the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough and the hon. member for Gloucester that the movement which is now under way and the representations which have recently been made to the government are not inspired by anything they may have said in this chamber. The movement has been under way for some weeks and the memorial which has been presented to the government sets forth fairly, I think, the position of the two provinces represented. I am not quite certain why the aid of Liberal members from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick was not sought. I do not know that it would have added to or detracted from the weight of the representations which have been made. Be that as it may, I do desire to remind this house and the country that ever since the declaration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1903, when he introduced the bill with respect to the construction of the Transcontinental railway, the people of the two eastern provinces have been waiting for the fulfilment of the promise he then made. Although it may have been quoted many times in this house, I desire to read very briefly the statement made at that time, upon which the appeal for the establishment of this rate is now based. The appeal made at that time is based chiefly on the statute under which the Transcontinental was built, and which specified that-

-the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin 'to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports.
That was the underlying principle of the rate structure to be established on tlm construction of the Transcontinental railway. That principle has never been adhered to from that time to this.
I am not blaming any political party or any particular government which has been in power. I am conscious of the fact that very important elements in our own country have been opposed to the establishment and carrying out of the principle underlying that declaration, and I venture to suggest that we do not have to look very much further than the port of Montreal as being the great deterrent to its fulfilment. They are fearful,
I think, of the loss of the traffic which they have enjoyed for many years past in the shipment of American grain through their port. That is natural, but it simply emphasizes the selfishness of the port interests of the city of Montreal. They are willing to fight for that selfish interest no matter what becomes of the rest of Canada or of the winter ports of the maritimes. We from the maritime provinces protest against the selfish attitude of the port of Montreal with respect to this whole question, and I say to my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Prime Minister and his government, let us try this matter out. Threats of retaliation should not deter a government from doing what is right if the principle involved is right. I know we are constantly under the economic pressure of the country to the south of us, but we are still a self-reliant nation; I have always noticed that when we stand up for our rights we gain their respect, and I believe that we shall continue to do so if we stand up for our rights in respect to this particular matter.
Let me say just this in conclusion. I did not take up a great deal of time in this house in days gone by when we were in opposition and dealing with the question of maritime rights; though I have sympathized with that movement and have spoken occasionally in favour of it, I have never taken up much of the time of this house discussing it or seeking newspaper publicity with regard to it. The people of the maritime provinces, certainly expect that the principle laid down as long ago as 1903, twenty-nine years ago, by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, shall now be brought to fruition. Matters are now coming to a climax. They feel that ample time has elapsed to make the necessary arrangements. All these huge expenditures which have been made for port facilities,

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
all these things which have been done recently as well as in former years and are now being done through the harbour commissions in St. John and Halifax, have been in preparation for the final carrying out of the principle implied in the Transcontinental railway legislation, and up to date they have all been practically a dead letter. Let all parties in this house get together and get behind the government and ask them to put this into effect at all events as a trial measure. The people of the maritime provinces will then know whether or not they are able to overcome geography, whether they are able to bring to fruition the hopes and aspirations of the last three decades.

Naturally I am much
interested in the discussion that has taken place this afternoon regarding the export of Canada's wheat and the channels through which it should go. I should like to ask the minister if his attention has been drawn to a new item appearing in this morning's Citizen, reading as follows:
Albany, N.Y., April 14.-A Canadian grain syndicate has signed a 10-year lease for the 2,500,000-bushel elevator planned for the port of Albany, it was revealed to-day when bids for the construction work were opened. The name of the syndicate was not revealed, but A. R. Roberts, of Toronto, its representative, said it had resources exceeding $60,000,000 and that it represented a combination of elevator and grain transportation groups. He said it controlled seven elevators and 20 lake steamers.
I would ask the minister if he has any knowledge of this transaction.

No more than my hon. friend has from the announcement he has just read. I should like to intimate to him that one should be a little cautious about attaching full weight to stories of that character. Merely to put the question to me, do I know anything about it or not, cannot get us anywhere. I know nothing about it, and the government knows nothing about it other than the statement which was made in the press. Of course we know, as everybody knows, that there have been many stories about the development of the port of Albany on the Hudson river, and all that sort of thing. There is the question of the deep waterways scheme. All these matters are being discussed in the press by persons, some responsible and some utterly irresponsible. I do not think that in considering the movement of our wheat crop we should be brought into any official contact with suggestions of the possible promotion by Americans or others of projects which are obviously of a private character. I would not like to leave in my answer to my hon. friend 41761-130
the impression that much importance should be attached to the announcement, which obviously is not and cannot be official.
I really must accept the statement in the press as being founded upon a possibility. However, I am willing to accept the statement of the minister that he knows nothing of the matter.
No, I do not.

In connection with this rate on grain to Halifax and St. John, I have been interested to know whether there is any discrimination against our Canadian ports as compared with American ports. Would the minister tell the committee what is the exact railway rate on grain from the head of the lakes to St. John and Halifax, as compared with the rate from the head of the lakes to New York, Boston and other American ports?

I cannot answer the question definitely at the moment, and perhaps it would be better for me not to reply to if offhand. But I am under the impression, and I give this for what it is worth, that the rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal is the same as from the head of the lakes to New York. When we come to Halifax and St. John we come to the special rates for winter haulage in connection with which two factors must be considered. One is the special rate to Quebec from the west of 18-34.
That is not for the winter months.
My hon. friend from Gloucester has said that is not for winter haulage; I am under the impression it is.
It is all the year round.

I was not discriminating in that sense. I had simply said that there was a rate to Quebec of 18-34. Then, there is a special rate to Halifax and St. John which is not as high as the normal rate governing the movement of freight, part of which is accounted for in the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Then there is the differential which is now complained of, and we have the arguments of the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the other hon. members who have spoken, asking for a one cent differential to be added to the Quebec rate which would put the mari-times on a much better basis.
While I am speaking may I say to the committee that this whole question is under study. The discussion this afternoon has been earnestly and effectively put forward by all speakers. I assure hon. members in the committee that as early as possible the matter

Supply-Trade-Grain Act

will be taken under advisement, and I express the hope that some decision may be arrived at in the near future. This matter is of tremendous importance. I do not wish to occupy the time of the committee in a long, detailed dissertation, but I assure hon. members that the question of grain is not the only matter under consideration. Many other elements which will be of advantage to the maritime ports may be worked out before long, at least before another session has passed. I can merely add that in the immediate future we will give the whole question the most earnest study.

If grain is to be shipped out of this country surely the shipper must know the freight rate from Fort William to Halifax as compared with the rate from Fort William to New York, because no farmers would ship grain to Halifax if it cost five or six cents more than to ship it to New York.
