I believe I should have the right now, as a lone voice from northern Ontario, to state the sentiments of my section of the country. I believe that most of the anomalies which have to be faced in the maritime provinces, would be removed if we could have shipments of grain over the transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec during the summer and winter. This is a very vital question to my section of the country, and as some speakers seem to have made it a political issue, I may say that I fully appreciate the position of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because -when I was sitting in support of this party when it was in power, I made representations to the government of that day. I fully realize the obstacles and difficulties which have to 'be surmounted. I believe that this question is capable of solution. I listened with a good deal of attention to
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou, and it seems to me that the port of Halifax could receive a fair share of the wheat traffic if the old transcontinental could get its quota of freight haulage. I remember, although I was a young man at the time, when in 1903 the charter was granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific. It was said at that time that this was going to provide the Shortest distance from ocean to ocean, and the road was going to haul heavy freight, such as grain and cattle, at a cheaper rate than the railway system as it then existed. The people were told that it was going to shorten the distance so considerably, that, as I remember, cartoons appeared in the Montreal Star suggesting that the Transcontinental line, under contemplation then, would be the shortest way to travel around the world. Sad to say, however, our expectations have not been fulfilled. As we all remember, the Transcontinental section from Quebec to Winnipeg was built by the federal government and was supposed to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific after completion. For reasons well known to the country as a whole, that fact has not been accomplished. The fact remains, nevertheless, that we have never had any real haulage of grain from the prairies to the eastern ports over that section of the road. This is the best section of road bed on the American continent. It is over one thousand miles long and the grades are excellent, so that haulage over that section could be done at a cheaper rate than on any other section of our railways.
This question is becoming more and more acute, particularly in Cochrane and along that section of the Transcontinental, because the people have seen the administration of the Canadian National-I will not discuss this point now-withdrawing passenger service from Montreal to Winnipeg by way of North Bay and Cochrane. In our section of the country last summer and fall we were astonished that the royal commission did not find it possible to have at least a brief sitting in the town of Cochrane, which is one of the divisional points on the Transcontinental, being half way between Quebec and Winnipeg. I hope that before the inquiry is over that commission will visit Cochrane and study for themselves, on the ground, the situation as it actually exists.
I wish to be as brief as possible, and for that reason I will quote some observations and newspaper articles that have been published in the past in regard to this matter. Let me read a short excerpt from a speech

made in 1917 by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Speaking at that time the hon. gentleman said:
The Transcontinental, sweeping from Winnipeg through northern Ontario to Cochrane, and thence over the boundary to Amos and down into Quebec city, provided the most direct route and the easiest gradients from the prairies to the St. Lawrence. Accordingly, when the road was completed in 1916, it was able to quote a rate of six cents per bushel on wheat from Armstrong-a station in the Thunder Bay district just west and north of Lake Nipigon, and almost due north of Fort William and Port Arthur-down to Quebec city, 959 miles distant.
But then a mysterious thing happened. Hardly had the rate been announced when the Conservative government almost quadrupled it.
The increased rate, it is alleged, proved not only discriminatory, but also prohibitive. The result was that the expected volume of traffic did not develop.
What was the reason for this startling increase in the schedule for wheat?
That is why I want to ask the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, as I asked the previous government, for support for this proposal. I want to impress upon the government as well as upon hon. members from the maritime provinces and from Quebec, the fact that enormous sums of money have been spent in the construction of the trans-Canada highway, which expenditure is not coming to fruition for the reason that we do not get our fair share of freight haulage.
Let me read a few paragraphs from a resolution passed by the Cochrane board of trade only a few months ago with respect to freight matters:

speechtext: Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the second reading of Bill No. 44, to amend the Railway Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: RAILWAY COMMISSION AND RATE STRUCTURE-SPECIAL COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I shall have to oppose this bill on principle because there are two or three ideas introduced which have not been observed in this country for many years. Section 1 of the bill adds the following words as subsection 2 of section 320 of the act:
The board may consider the question of what should be reasonable compensation under the circumstances, and may establish a rate structure in the interests of trade development and public policy, though such experimental rates may not at the time or of themselves give reasonable compensation to the railway companies.
It is proposed by this section to give to the Board of Railway Commissioners a power which in the past has always been entirely in the hands of the government of the day, the power of developing trade and the formulation of general public policies. In other words, we would be permitting the Board of Railway Commissioners to take unto itself the matter of the trade of this country, which matter belongs to the government and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No government in the past has ever suggested that the formulation of such policies shall be put in the hands of an outside body. This objection in itself is sufficient to condemn the bill from the standpoint of any government, whether the present government or the one which preceded it. Section 2 of the bill reads as follows:
Subsection five of section three hundred and twenty-five of the said act is amended by striking out the proviso thereto and substituting the following therefor:
"Provided that, notwithstanding anything in this subsection contained, rates on grain and flour shall, on and from the twenty-seventh day of June, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five, be governed by the provisions of the agreement made pursuant to chapter five of the statutes of Canada, 1897, but such rates shall apply to all such traffic moving from ail points on all lines of railway west of Fort William to Fort William or Port Arthur-
Then come the words suggested to be inserted :
-and to all such traffic moving westwardly from Fort William, and from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William, to Vancouver, British Columbia and to ports on the Pacific coast,-*
And then follows the wording of the old section:
-over all lines now or hereafter constructed by any company subject to the jurisdiction of parliament."
I suggest that that section means that rates shall be fixed without a hearing being given to the railway companies or to other inter-
Railway Act

ested parties. If I understand rightly, I think the intention is to put into force all the Crowsnest rates westward. The hon. member nods assent, so apparently I have interpreted correctly. This parliament has no facilities for the making of rates. I admit that in the past, I think it was 1897, parliament did by statute fix the Crowsnest rates, but that was done in agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and was in return for the fulfilment of certain conditions by that company. As a general rule parliament has always taken the attitude that it does not fix rates. I consider this to be the right attitude because parliament, constituted as it is, is not capable of going into such a complicated matter as the freight rate structure of this country. That question is perhaps the most complicated with which anyone has to deal, and early in the present century the Board of Railway Commissioners was constituted for the purpose of giving its full time to the study of the question. The board is the proper body to which to apply for such rate fixing as is covered by this bill.
Thus there are two principles invaded by this bill. The first is to hand over to the Board of Railway Commissioners the forming of the trade policy of the government, which is a matter purely within the jurisdiction of the government through the Department of Trade and Commerce. Secondly, the bill attempts to fix rates, something which has never before been attempted by the parliament of Canada in such a bill as this. Certainly rates should not be fixed without giving an opportunity to be heard not only to the consumer, to whom the hon. member referred, but to the railways themselves. The two principles involved in the second reading of this bill cannot be accepted, in fairness to the railways, in fairness to the people, and in fairness to the parliament of Canada itself.
There is at the present time a royal commission sitting in Canada, appointed to look into the whole transportation question. No one knows at the moment what the recommendations of that commission will be, and it is quite possible that it may offer suggestions Which would alter the scope of this bill. In view of what I have pointed out, I suggest to my hon. friend in the friendliest way possible that he might be well advised to withdraw the bill for the present session and hold it over until the next session of parliament. It is possible and even probable that the next session may be called at a date earlier than has been the case in past years, and my hon. friend would not have to wait very long for an opportunity to bring in a bill which would

comply with the points I have mentioned.
I appeal to the hon. gentleman, in the spirit of fair play which I hope he will show in this regard, to let this bill stand over until next session. By that time he will have had time to look thoroughly into the question and to deal with it in such a way that the recognized principles of rate making which have been in existence in Canada for many years shall not be infringed.

Mr. Speaker, I am familiar only with the general principles of this bill. I cannot understand why a request should be made to defeat it on the grounds of fair play. I do not think the question of unfairness is involved in this bill;
I submit that t-he unfairness has existed in connection with the rates prevailing on shipments to British Columbia. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has stated that this bill would give too much power to the railway board, and suggests that it is the duty of the government to deal with matters of this kind. If so the government has failed signally for some considerable time to fulfil its duty; I allude to the standing grievance of British Columbia in connection with the discrimination in the rates between grain for export and those for domestic consumption. Blame can be laid at the doors of both the present and past governments, the net result being that this discrimination has been in effect for something like six years. If now is not the time to take action, I do not know when it will be. It is suggested we should consider it between now and next fall. I submit that we have already had ample time in which to discuss it. If I am not mistaken, the hon. member who introduced the bill quoted the other day from the Duncan report, which specifically recommends the very phraseology which has been inserted in this bill, in one section at any rate. The Duncan report was very highly approved by very many people, and by far the greater part of its provisions have been carried into effect.
As regards fixing rates, which the minister deplores, he himself says there is precedent for that. He does not need to go so far back as the initiation of the Crowsnest pass rate, because it was renewed again in 1923 or 1924, and this bill seeks not to fix rates or make new ones, but only to authorize the railway board to extend the principle of the rates there suggested and carried out. He used the words "to fix rates." I would not say "to fix rates"; it is to equalize rates, only to make the rates westward the same as they are eastward on similar goods and under similar conditions.

Railway Act
He suggests that vve should await the report of the royal commission. That commission is dealing with transportation in its broadest aspect and is extremely unlikely to make any specific recommendation regarding rates. Meanwhile we do not know when it will report or what the nature of the report will be, or anything else. But we have before us a gross outstanding grievance from which the people of British Columbia have suffered for quite a number bf years. There is no reason why we should not put our hands to the plough to remedy it now; it is there and obvious, and apparently this is the proper method. The Duncan 'Commission and other authorities have said that if we ever expect the Board of Railway Commissioners to give us that justice for which we ask in British Columbia, some language such as this will have to be inserted in the bill to give them the authority, because at the present time it is lacking. I think some members of the railway board, in the course of decisions rendered, indicated that their ruling would have to be adverse to our just desires and interests because of the lack of authority which they pointed out and which is, by this bill, sought to be given to -them. I am surprised the bill has not had some active support, not only from western members whose interests are identical with ours in British Columbia, though coming from the other end of the journey so to apeak, but also from other British Columbia members.

If the hon. member who has introduced the bill intends to press it, I desire to say a word with regard to it. I am opposed, first of all, to the whole principle of making special rates for the movement of commodities in any part of the country. General business in many parts suffers more than anything else from what has taken place in the last twenty years in making special rates for particular commodities in certain parts of the country. This bill in its general outline proposes to introduce what is known as the Crowsnest pass rates on all commodities moving westward from Fort William to the Pacific coast, leaving aside altogether the amendments which are proposed to section 320. It should, I think, be obvious to anyone who has given thought to the transportation problem of Canada that if the railways are to continue to operate, they must get somewhere a sufficient revenue to pay the bill. That revenue can be secured in just two ways, either by the people whose commodities are moving paying the cost of moving them, or by the general public paying through their general taxes
for the movement of those commodities, At the present time, on one line of railways, the Canadian National, this payment is being made partly in one way and partly in another. The person who moves commodities or who travels on the Canadian National lines pays part of the cost of operation; the general public pays the balance, an amount that since the railway was taken over by the Canadian people has been approxiately $75,000,000- a year. As regards the Canadian Pacific, up to the present moment the people whose commodities are moving have paid the entire cost. If we are to get down to a sound business basis, the commodity that is being moved must pay the cost of moving it; but by such measures as the one now before the house the railway commission is virtually given instructions to make special rates on particular commodities in certain sections of the country. This means that if the railways are to secure sufficient income to pay wages and meet the cost of coal, oil and all manner of operating expenses, some other commodity in some other part of the country must carry the load. Without desiring to criticize what has been done in the past I may say that rates have been made-and perhaps rightly so; I am not at the moment going to dispute the principle-to favour special commodities in particular parts while other commodities in other parts must bear the burden. Within the last few minutes I have taken occasion to get the comparative rates on one particular commodity on western and eastern lines of Canadian railways. A British Columbia lumberman can now move a carload of lumber 1,200 miles for the same cost that an Ontario or Quebec or New Brunswick lumberman can move a carload of lumber 800 miles. If this bill is passed, then the Ontario, Quebec or New Brunswick lumberman will have to bear an additional cost or some other shipper of another commodity will have to bear it to equalize the loss of revenue involved in putting these rates into effect.
If I correctly understood the hon. member who introduced the bill, when he spoke on the first reading he indicated it was his judgment that reduced rates would increase the movement of traffic and the railroads would make more money. That may be quite true; I am not going to dispute it. It may be that the hon. member understands the incidence of railway earnings and what will increase them better than Sir Henry Thornton or Mr. E. W. Beatty or the traffic officers of the two railways, but I am somewhat doubtful and I maintain that before an enactment of this kind is passed, at least the traffic officers of
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

the railway commission should determine what the effect is going to be in that regard. Before any legislation is passed in the house creating special rates or conditions for any commodity in any part of the country, the whole rate structure should be recast on a basis that will be equitable to all commodities and to all parts of Canada. Special legislation creating particular rates for one commodity or one part of the country has, as I said a moment ago, bedevilled the whole rate structure and made it impossible for business to be conducted on an equitable basis. I am opposed in principle to a measure of this kind. Instead of removing discrimination, it can have no other effect than to increase it as between one commodity and another and one part of Canada and another.

at six o'clock I was pointing out the opportunity which the National Transcontinental railway affords for more direct communication from ocean to ocean and the need for a greater amount of traffic being routed over that road. It has been suggested that the reason we have not our proper share of through freight traffic for the transcontinental is found in physical conditions. Last summer I spent three weeks making an inquiry into this phase of the matter, and I should like to give to the committee the information I gathered in regard to the physical obstructions we have to face in our section of the country.
A very misleading and detrimental opinion seems to be that northern Ontario and northern Quebec suffer from unusual climatic conditions. As a matter of fact the temperatures in these parts compare favorably with much older and more settled parts of the country. The snowfall is invariably lighter, and although we sometimes experience lower temperatures, they are not constant, and the air being dry, the cold does not affect one nearly as much as a damper climate with higher temperatures.
The Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway and that portion of the Canadian National Railways known as the transcon-

tinental have operated through northern Ontario and northern Quebec for some years and do not suffer traffic delays owing to climatic conditions. Trains Nos. 1 and 2 of the Canadian National Railways operated over these lines for the past twelve years wdth practically no delays chargeable to weather conditions, and maintained their schedules without difficulty.
Prior to the construction of the Nakina-Longlae cut-off, which connected the transcontinental railway-with the former Canadian Northern Railway, that portion of the Canadian National railway stretching from Winnipeg to Quebec city, some 1,300 miles, enjoyed a period of prosperity and showed a profit over and above operating costs of approximately forty cents on the dollar. Owing to the extremely low grades and slight curvatures through this portion of the country, heavy tonnage and long freight trains make for profitable operation. Solid trains of stock were moved over this line in trains of seventy-five cars and at a speed which saved the expense of unloading and feeding once between Winnipeg and Montreal, which in itself means much in shrinkage and expense to shippers when one considers there are twenty-five to thirty head of stock per car.
Grain was moved over the transcontinental line at a rate of eleven cents per hundredweight and moved at a profit, on account of these favourable conditions.
In comparison with the grades on the Canadian Pacific railway, Algoma district,, across the same portion of the country,, although much further south and through hillier territory, the same class of engines actually handle only one-third the tonnage handled by the same power over the transcontinental line.
Since the building of the Longlac-Nakina cut-off the portion of the transcontinental, .between Nakina and Quebec has existed on purely local traffic, made up of pulpwood, construction .material and manufacturing materials such as sulphur, coal, lime, and so forth, for the manufacturing plants located along this line, and even under these conditions the road operates at a profit, although a reduced one.
The Transcona elevator, originally built to clean grain and supply the transcontinental line with traffic has never been used to any extent. It would avoid moving the grain to the lake head for cleaning and give the western shippers a shorter route to the ocean ports, a saving in tonnage which would benefit the east as well as the west.

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
I well remember seventeen years ago the big celebration we had in Cochrane when the first national transcontinental train came in from Toronto. At that time we visualized through passenger and freight traffic going over that transcontinental section of the line, but we have been sadly disillusioned. We have not got that traffic, for reasons which are unknown to the people of northern Ontario, unless it is discriminatory rates. I listened with a good deal of attention to the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon stating that the government has absolutely nothing to do with the routing of the grain. I appreciate that, nevertheless we feel that if there had not been a discriminatory rate against the transcontinental route from Winnipeg to Quebec city and the maritime provinces we would have received a fair share of the through traffic during the last fifteen years. It has been mentioned this afternoon by members from the maritime provinces that at a certain period during the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific the whole project was jeopardized on account of the fact that the grades had been tampered with, or that they were not being built up to the highest standard possible from ocean to ocean. That condition does not apply on the transcontinental section from Winnipeg to Quebec, because luckily most of that construction iwas done under the regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I should like to read a clipping from the Halifax Mail which I think is well worthy of the attention of the house. Under the heading "A forgotten Railway," this paper says:
Discussing the memorial of the Cochrane (Ontario) Board of Trade ("vigorously seconded" by the maritime provinces), the Winnipeg Free Press has some pointed comment to make on "a forgotten railway policy."

I would
remind the hon. gentleman that we are discussing the administration of the Canada Grain Act.

With all due respect
to you, Mr. Chairman, I submit that my remarks are no more out of order than many of the speeches we heard this afternoon. The hon. member will please come to his point.

My point, Mr. Chairman, is that the transcontinental is not being
given a fair share of the through grain traffic from Winnipeg to Quebec and the maritime provinces. I will continue with the quotation:

"Having regard to the use to which the road has been put, it can only be assumed that this railway was built by tlie country in a fit of absent-mindedness. Before the road was finished, the country forgot what it was all about; and not only has no effort been made to put it to the purpose for which it was built, but difficulties in the way of permitting it being applied to these purposes have been encouraged."
"Looking back twenty-five years or fifty, it is clear that the railway scheme, with which the people appeared so fascinated in 1904, has thus far been disastrous to the country. There must be an anomaly somewhere, and the house should enter into a thorough discussion of the matter and endeavour to

supply a remedy. The people of Canada who are not familiar with railroad matters and with matters of commerce are asking questions. They do not know why it is not possible to direct some of the traffic over the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian National.
To make my point clear, and to be as brief as possible, I shall read to the house some of the reasons why in my section of the country there is dissatisfaction. I have before me an editorial from the Cochrane Northland Post, which I have no doubt will give food for thought to some hon. members in this house. It is as follows:
Any really satisfactory solution of this gigantic problem must necessarily include two features; the utilizing of the lowest haulage-cost sections to their full capacity, and an increase in freight traffic. Other features such as mutually advantageous cooperation between the two great railway systems will have their place in the solution, but these two are of paramount importance.
In dealing with the matter of increased freight traffic, it may, at first, seem illogical to speak of increasing freight traffic in a wide spread country such as Canada with its just a trifle more than 10,000,000 people. But in the year 1930, according to Colonel C. E. Phinney, President of the Halifax Harbour Commissioners, "Canadian grain moving eastward for export during the past year (1930) has been handled through the following channels:
Via Canadian ports-47,300,000 bushels.
Via United States ports-67,700,000 bushels."
And speaking at Halifax last October, Colonel Phinney quoted an editorial indicating that "transportation of 1,000,000 bushels of grain over the National Transcontinental to an Atlantic port would cause the expenditure of $53,000 for labour and $10,000 for fuel.''
Thus, if, in 1930, the 67 million bushels of grain which was exported via the United States had been shipped over the National Transcontinental line over 38 millions of dollars more would have been paid to Canadian workers. Why should this money, so greatly needed by our own workers, be paid into the pockets of workers across the border? The continuation of such a situation is inimical to the welfare of the country and intolerable to the pride of the people of Canada. And that there has been no effort made to remedy this disgraceful state of affairs is shown by the fact that in August and September of 1931 (the first two months of the 1931-32 crop year), wheat shipments of Canadian grain to the United Kingdom left Canada as follows:
Via Canadian Atlantic	ports-2,781,810
bushels.
Via Canadian Pacific ports-2,454,455 bushels.
Via United States ports-11,796,785 bushels, or over twice as much Canadian grain was exported through American channels as through Canadian channels. Such a condition must be irritating in the extreme to Canadian railway and port workers on short time and many without work at all. If it requires a royal commission to right wrongs such as this, surely it is about time that we had new administration for our railways.

There can be no excuse, no justification for this execrable wrong to Canadian ports and Canadian workers. The Dominion government by act of parliament, decreed in the N.T.R. Act:
"The through rate on traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports." In his Halifax speech above referred to Colonel Phinney said:
"The railway built to carry this grain" (Colonel Phinney was referring to the National Transcontinental), "has cost us $330,000,000, and I say we should not sit down and do nothing about it while deficits pile up year after year, on a railway for which we have paid and are still paying, and which is not being operated.
"Isn't it better, for example, to lose a sum of money each year on the railway and have it in operation, than to lose the same sum and not have it in operation? The traffic this road could carry is going through American ports and over American railways, and I ask if it would not be better business to go over our own lines and through our own ports."
When the Canadian railways were caught in the act of transporting Russian pulp to American markets, which was directly competing with our own Canadian product, they offered the excuse that they needed the traffic, and yet here is a vast amount of home grown traffic slipping through their hands into American channels. To paraphrase the song, Do you call this Ganadianism?
We believe that the majority of Canadians are whole hearted ly behind the Canadian National railways. We all, or nearly all of us, have faith in it and believe that it will succeed."
Oh, oh.

should be more respectful. I have spoken very little this session and I submit I should be allowed to state the case for northern Ontario. Hon. members have spoken on behalf of the maritime provinces, and I intend to speak for northern Ontario. I may take a half hour more. The: article continues.
But it must be operated for the benefit of the Canadian people. Here in the National Transcontinental line, we have a railroad designed and built to carry heavy trains with a minimum of motive power, a line over which western grain can be hauled to Atlantic ports cheaper than over any other line. In the name of common sense, why is this fine not used for the purpose for which it was designed and built? Why is Canadian grown grain, which could be transported over this line cheaper than over any other line, diverted to American channels with the consequent loss to Canadian railways and to Canadian workers?
This matter is not just a local one. It affects Canada as a whole. When Canadian workers are deprived of earnings to the extent of over 38 millions of dollars in one year, it is the concern of all Canada. When traffic, which could be economically handled over a railway line built

and paid for by the Canadian public, is diverted to foreign channels, the people of Canada have a right to ask why.
What are the railway heads going to do about this? What about our members of parliament?
From the discussion which has taken place to-day it would seem that the maritime provinces, the province of Quebec and northern Ontario are very much interested. To-day a condition exists along the Transcontinental railway from Quebec to Winnipeg wherein thousands of men who were working on the railroad for the last eighteen years have been thrown out of employment. When they read articles such as this disclosing the fact that fifty per cent of our grain production reaches American ports, dissatisfaction must arise in their minds. In my view it is only right and proper that the matter should be discussed on the floor of the House of Commons.
I said at the, beginning of my remarks that I did not intend to discuss the matter from a political standpoint, but rather to bring it before the house merely as a condition which must be faced. I greatly appreciated the statements by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I feel sure he will do his utmost to arrive at a solution. I listened with equal interest to the remarks of the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said that the situation was both delicate and intricate. At the same time I maintain Canada should do all in its power to obtain its share of the through traffic.
At this point I should like to read a letter from the Telegraph-Journal and the Evening Times-Globe of St. John, New Brunswick. This letter is dated April 6, 1932 and is as follows:
Dear Sir:
The United States Department of Commerce recently announced that on the average 49 per cent or approximately one-half of Canada's wheat and flour export trade has been handled through United States ports during the last six years.
Practically no wheat has passed through eastern Canadian ports during the last winter season, and our information is that during the summer months almost the entire Canadian crop routed east went to Buffalo.
We beg to draw your attention to the enclosed editorial, published to-day in the Telegraph-Journal and the Evening Times-Globe and to urge upon you the gravity of this situation.
We feel that you, in your public capacity, can strike a blow for the people whom you represent in parliament by standing for the formulation of and strict adherence to national transportation policy which will divert this valuable trade stream from foreign channels
to Canadian railways and Canadian ports, and thus give much needed employment to thousands of Canadian citizens.
The people of Canada are being urged continuously to buy Canadian goods, and thereby employ Canadian labour. In our judgment, Canadian labour includes Canadian railway men and Canadian port workers as fully as it concerns itself with the employees of manufacturing plants.	.
We feel that men in public life can render no greater service to our country at the present time than by doing their utmost to correct this most unpatriotic and uneconomic condition of affairs.
Yours very truly,
F. X. Jennings, Acting Editor-in-Chief.
This letter pictures the situation existing with regard to our national railways. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will do his utmost to have his department solve this problem, and, if that is not possible, then some other department, the Railway department for example, should, in my opinion, take steps to meet the situation, so that we shall receive justice in the maritime provinces and also in Ontario. I trust that we shall receive the quota of traffic to which we are entitled, and in that way the situation, which is becoming graver and graver, will be remedied.
I mentioned a short while ago that only yesterday I received a letter from a clergyman of Cochrane deploring the fact that even now, after having been in suspense for several months, employees of the Canadian National Railways who have been in their service fifteen and eighteen years are being laid off- carmen, trainmen, and various other men employed on the road. I repeat that if we were getting our fair share of freight transportation over the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec there would be no railroad unemployment in our section of the country. I sincerely hope that the government will find some solution for this problem. We talk of national policies in this country; a good deal is said about the "Canada first" policy. Well, I submit to the minister that this should be one of the first principles to apply to the railways and our harbour facilities, namely, that we should receive that fair quota of transportation to which we are entitled.

What is the justification of
the Department, of Trade and Commerce buying a patriotic picture?
First, because the department is patriotic; second, because the administration of that particular activity is under the department.
Has the picture ever left the vaults of the department?
Yes.
I have grave doubts as to that. I think the minister had better make inquiries. Did the officials of the department recommend its purchase?
I have not that information before me.

During the conversion
loan advertising campaign I noticed extensive advertising through the medium of both silent and talking pictures. Would that naturally come out of last year's expenditure under this item?
No; all the advertising in connection with loans would be paid by the Department of Finance. Sometimes this department will take pictures for other departments.

Item agreed to.
Weights and Measures inspection service, including the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, $310,200.

May I make a suggestion
to the minister? If I am not mistaken, at the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
present time the charge for inspecting weights is $10, and this is paid by those whose weights are right as well as by those whose weights are wrong. Would the minister consider this suggestion: to charge less to those whose weights or measures are right, and more to those whose weights or measures are wrong?
That seems like a reasonable suggestion. I shall look into it and confer with the officials who have wide experience in the matter.

I thank the minister for
his answer. The suggestion comes from a country merchant who told me that one day he received a visit from an inspector who inspected his balance. The balance could weigh, say 200 pounds and with the weights he was carrying with him, the inspector tested it to forty pounds and found it correct. As a matter of fact the balance was wrong from fifty pounds up, but the inspector marked it
O.K., and then the merchant refused to pay the $10. The inspector asked him why, and the merchant told him it was because the inspection was wrong, which he proceeded to prove. This is why I am drawing the matter to the attention of the minister.
Is any revenue derived from this service?

There is a surplus every
year of about $60,000.

Does the department
supply the weights and measures inspectors in western Canada with a car, or allow them mileage to drive from place to place?
They are allowed mileage when it is required in the country places.

What is the mileage
paid?

I am informed that it is
from eight to ten cents per mile.
How many inspectors are there ?
There are 115.

Item agreed to.
Exhibitions and fairs, including the sum of $750, required by the Department of Immigration and Colonization, $137,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

This is the usual vote for exhibitions. A substantial portion of the item is expended on regular exhibitions in Great Britain in the large industrial centres, and so forth, devoted almost entirely to exhibiting Canadian produce generally, lumber, fish, fruit, flour and all that class of goods. I can give the details of expenditures if required, but this is the usual vote. There is very little variation from year to year in the type of fair that is patronized. Occasionally a large fair or exhibition is involved, but there is no provision in this vote for exhibiting at any large fair.
We sent people down to the Argentine to represent the Canadian government at an exhibition there a year or two ago. Would that come under this vote?
There was a special vote for that.

The only thing I
wanted to remark in that connection was that before we sent our representatives to that exhibition we were selling to the Argentine $12,000,000 worth of produce annually, and the year after that exhibition we sold them only $-1,000,000 worth. If we send another such delegation with no better results, we shall soon be selling the Argentine nothing at all.

What is the $750 for
which is required by the Department of Immigration?

That is more or less a
vanishing item. Years ago the Immigration department did require certain small exhibits to be displayed in windows, made up by experts under this department, but that is virtually finished. This is just a small vote for some places they have left.

There is a decrease of
$148,000 in this vote as compared with last year. How is that accounted for?

There are no large fairs
provided for under this item-just a number of routine exhibits.

Item agreed to.
Dominion Bureau of Statistics, $512,000.
I assume the decrease in this item is due to the census work having passed the peak.
It is due to the tapering off of the census work.
Item agreed to.
Supply-Railways and Canals

Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited
Loan to .the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited, repayable on demand with interest at a rate to be fixed by the Governor in council, upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine, and to be applied in payment of: -
Deficts in operation of the company and the vessels under the company's control during the year ended December 31, 1931, and interest requirements. Additional amount required in excess of the sum of $755,000 already appropriated, $161,568.53.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: This is a supplementary item which has passed the special committee.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway and terminals: construction and betterments, including E- B. Jost at $2,250 (revote $630,000), $1,937,700.
Is this to complete?

It just depends on what we mean by complete. It would hardly be correct to say that it would complete the work, but it will put the port in condition to carry on with any reasonable amount of shipping that may go out there this year. Briefly, it will build a shed which will be necessary to handle package freight of any kind, it will complete the work on the elevator so that it can handle quite a large amount of grain; it will do some work on the water supply, do some filling and some dredging and considerable work on the Hudson Bay railway itself, such as ballasting and levelling up the road, which is always necessary in that country after the winter's settling. In general it will put the whole system in shape to handle any reasonable amount of traffic that may go over it this coming year.
Is it contemplated building docks there for coal?

There is a dock eighteen hundred feet long, at one end of which there is plenty of room to store coal. There is no intention of putting up a special dock or getting special equipment this year for handling coal. There are two locomotive cranes which can handle any coal which may come in there this coming season. If it is shown throughout the season that there is likely to be a heavy amount of coal coming in through that port later, it is the intention in the coming years to build a complete dock, 'but with our present equipment we can handle any coal that may come in from either Nova Scotia or Great Britain this season.
What freight rate was charged on the trial shipment going over that route?
'It was all charged on the Crowsnest basis to the head of the lakes.
Was that rate made by the government?

No, the government does not make rates. The rates were made in this case by the Canadian National Railway itself, subject of course to revision by the Board of Railway Commissioners. I adhere to what I said earlier in the evening, that the government does not make rates.

From what I gather in the press, I understand that some difficulty was experienced last year in securing this first shipment of grain to go out over the Hudson Bay route, that different grain companies and other people shipping grain seemed dubious about sending it over the route, which did not exactly bear out their enthusiasm for the route in the first place. Without my putting a lengthy series of questions to the minister, would he give us a brief statement as to the success of that trial shipment, the amount of grain handled, the terms and conditions on which it was handled, the costs borne by the government, and the result from the point of view of the shipper.

I shall gladly answer the hon. member. I shall have to resort to my memory, but I think it is quite clear in this connection, because I was deeply interested. The hon. member is quite right: last year we had considerable difficulty obtaining anything in the shape of grain cargoes. In fact I will tell now that which I did not state publicly last year, namely, that we communicated with various organizations, both public and private, in western Canada, and we had no success whatever so far as securing grain shipments was concerned. We took considerable abuse because we had not obtained grain shipments, despite the fact that we had done everything in our power to get them. At last we went to John I. McFarland-I do not know his position-
Manager of the central selling agency.
Yes,-who was appointed by my leader, the right the hon. Prime Minister.

Oh, oh.
* Mr. MANION: Mr. McFarland came to the city of Ottawa-

The minister has just admitted what the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not admit.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
Well, perhaps I used the wrong word.
No, your statement is absolutely true.

I am quite sure Mr. McFarland was suggested by the Prime Minister; perhaps I should have put it that way. It is quite possible the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows more than I do in regard to the selling agency as it comes within his purview. Probably I slipped that word in without going into the question. I frankly admit that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is correctly informed concerning Mr. McFarland's appointment, and I shall withdraw my remark.
However, to get back to my statement, may I say that Mr. McFarland held the position of manager of the selling agency. He came to the city of Ottawa and after the solicitation of the Prime Minister and myself-I might say the pleading-we got Mr. McFarland to supply us with two cargoes of grain to be shipped via Churchill.
Is that how it came about that Mr. McFarland bought wheat for future delivery?

My hon. friend had better ask Mr. McFarland about that. He supplied two cargoes. Then, while the government was not in the shipping business, and had nothing to do with the chartering of ships, and should have had nothing to do with business of that nature, in an effort to have a trial shipment through the port of Churchill we chartered two boats and guaranteed to Mr. McFarland that the handling would cost no more than if shipped via Montreal. The boats went in and handled the grain very successfully. Delivery of the elevator was made on the fifteenth; loading was commenced the same evening and continued until the ships were completely filled and trimmed. The experiment was quite successful, and my understanding is that the cost was slightly lower than it would have been had the grain been shipped via Montreal. I may add that we were to absorb port charges, elevator charges and any other charges which ordinarily would have been levied. Outside of that every charge was paid, including insurance, which was rather heavy. In every way the sending of these cargoes via Churchill was a complete success.
Could the minister give us an idea how insurance rates via Hudson Bay compare with those via Montreal?

I cannot say exactly, but they are considerably heavier. I believe the rate is about five times as much, perhaps six times, via Churchill as it is via Montreal. I can say at least that that condition prevailed last year.
While I am on my feet I should like to add that through the office of the Canadian High Commissioner at London we have taken up the matter of insurance rates. The Department of Marine has also investigated the matter because it is directly in>
control of insurance. The Canadian High Commissioner's office at London has passed the matter on to the Imperial shipping committee, in whose hands it now rests. My best information at the moment is that no reduction has been made. It has been more or less promised, however, that if shipments this year are as successful as those of last year, there will be a reduction in insurance rates in 1933. I am afraid that there is not a very great prospect of a reduction this year.
I heard the minister mention the fifteenth of a certain month, but I did not hear the month.
September.

I should like to ask the minister if he -oan tell us whether any steps are being taken to ensure further and perhaps more complete trial shipments in the coming
season.

Yes, every effort has been made. I must admit quite frankly, however, that we have not been very successful. A series of letters has been sent to grain dealers throughout western Canada. Shipping agents from Montreal have gone through the western provinces endeavouring to work up shipments. They assure me that they 'think there will probably be about ten or twelve ships go out of Churchill in the coming year. Frankly it has been very difficult to get cargoes going out or coming in. One shipping company, the Dalgleish Company-the same people who handled the shipment last year-have offered to take cargoes into Churchill on the same basis as the Montreal rate, provided they can get 1,000 tons, or about one-fifth of a cargo, to take in. In spite of that fact it has not been easy to arrange shipments. We have received very little encouragement, and these shipping agents have had difficulty in securing cargoes.

Does that cover
insurance, too?

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
Yes. They are hopeful that ten or a dozen ships will go into Churchill, which would constitute a pretty fair trial in the coming year.
Would there be any doubt about having wheat at the port, in case shipments had to be made?
There will not be trial shipments until there is wheat to go out.
If the boats are ready to take those shipments out-
The boats will not go unless the wheat is there.
I shall put the question another way: if wheat is there the boats will go?

The wheat will be there only if some agency in western Canada does as Mr. McFarland did last year. That is, some agent in western Canada must sell wheat, as Mr. McFarland did. We are not shipping wheat, because we are not handling it.

The minister must admit that the government will not guarantee bottoms to any western grain shipper shipping out of Churchill. You guaranteed Mr. McFarland two bottoms in which to ship his grain. In other words he guaranteed you the grain to make trial shipment.

There will be no difficulty whatever in getting bottoms. The difficulty is not to get bottoms or to get rates equal to those of Montreal; it is to get cargoes. There will be no difficulty getting cargoes if-
But-
Will the minister-
If my hon. friends will ask their questions one at a time I shall have a better chance to answer. Just now three or four questions are being asked at once from different sections of the chamber.
What difficulty will be encountered at Churchill?

The difficulty seems to be that western Canada shippers are not enthusiastic about shipping through the port of Churchill, and are not anxious to make arrangements to do so. The late government and the present one-I divide the credit- have put the port into good shape. We had no machinery for shipments; we had no machinery for buying and selling grain in this country and marketing it in Europe, or for

chartering vessels. We went out of our way and put this machinery into operation, because we felt it would be a black eye to Churchill if we did not do it. There is no difficulty whatever about getting ships provided the cargoes are there. I do not wish to be misquoted, but I am very hopeful that there will be sufficient to give ten or twelve cargoes out of Churchill this year. If there are cargoes there will be no difficulty about getting the ships.
Has the minister offered the people any consideration at all in the way of reducing the elevator handling charges, or is there the same arrangement as there was last year?
There was no charge last year, so that we cannot very well reduce it.
Then you have the same arrangement?

We have not had anything put up to us along that line. We will do everything we can, and gladly, to encourage anyone to utilize the port this coming year. As I have said, however, we cannot reduce the charge because there was none last year.

Does not my hon. friend think that it is the excessive insurance rate that terrifies the prospective shippers? They do not like to take a chance. Has the government thought of carrying part of the insurance until the port has had a real chance to work out?

I do not think my hon. friend is right in saying that the excessive insurance rate frightens people, because after all what people look at is the through rate, including insurance. What they consider, for instance, is the rate from Saskatoon, which would probably be the shipping point to Liverpool; they would take that rate, via Churchill, and compare it with the rate from Saskatoon to Liverpool via Montreal, and if the rate, inclusive of insurance, were lower via Churchill than via Montreal, it should be attractive to people wishing to ship grain. As regards absorbing insurance, whether I have thought of this matter or not, it has been forced upon my attention. But may I say it is not an easy matter to settle, for this reason. If that were the only thing that held up shipments via Churchill, it would be the duty of the government to do something in that regard, as a trial; but in my opinion that is not the reason that may make it difficult to get cargoes. It is probably a question of world depression, and general business con-

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
ditions. The difficulty arises again in regard to the absorption by the government of insurance so far as the other ports are concerned. The other ports, both east and west, would rightly say, "Why should the insurance be absorbed in one port and not in another?" Montreal or Quebec would probably come forward with such a representation. They might say, "If you are going to absorb insurance from Churchill, why not absorb it from Montreal and Quebec?" It is not therefore an easy matter to settle, and we do not wish to grapple with that problem unless it is absolutely necessary. And I do not think it is necessary, because the rate this year will be as low as the Montreal rate, if not lower. There was a difference of about two cents per bushel last year.

Trade and traffic
will not as a rule seek a new port unless there is some advantage to induce shippers to do so. Switching traffic from one route to another is a very difficult thing and takes a considerable time to accomplish. When the Panama canal route was first opened, via Vancouver, it remained open quite a while before there was any considerable traffic, especially of grain. Experimental shipments were made there too, as there was a fear at that time that the waters of the southern Pacific would have a deleterious effect upon the keeping qualities of wheat in transit, particularly if it had excess moisture. These difficulties were overcome and elevators constructed, but it must have been six or seven years before any considerable volume of traffic went through that port-a port open the year round. They had high mountain rates to overcome at that time also, there were no Crowsnest rates going then to the Pacific. That was no doubt a handicap. But here is the point. The government, if this route is to be successful, must do something to overcome the fears of the people with respect to rates and all the vicissitudes or possibilities of any new route, I do not care where it is. The route by the Panama occasioned fear because of the warmth of the water, and we can understand that the northern route might occasion fear because of the coldness of the water or because of the presence of icebergs or growlers or whatever there is to make people fearful; and unless there is a considerable volume of cargo produced, pressing for an exit, that port will be very slow developing without the sympathetic support of the government. Its development, I say, will be slow unless the government gives it considerable sympathetic
and tangible support of a practical nature such as I have indicated. The minister must realize that this is the history of trade the world over. It takes a great amount of effort and time to swing trade from one route to another, and there must be a good deal of cargo offering and pressing for a favourable exit before switching can possibly be made. The government, I repeat, should show us a more sympathetic consideration of a practical sort in the direction I have indicated, otherwise, for a long time to come, that port will not be used to any considerable extent. It will not be as fully used as it might be, because shippers will not use any new route to an appreciable extent until the advantages and risks are more fully known.

I remember that when the Panama route was first opened there was a fear in regard to the effect of the warm waters of the Pacific on grain. To-day, however, there is no such fear in connection with the northern route; in fact the northern waters will rather make it a safe route from that point of view. I think my hon. friend will admit that his government when in power and this government as well have shown great sympathy with the route. Last year we did, as we are doing this year, everything possible to encourage its utilization. I made inquiries to find out how much it would cost to send a ship for one trip. Suppose we sent a ship on the off chance of a cargo; it would cost from $30,000 to $40,000, and that is a nice figure to juggle with unless you are sure of your cargo. May I make a suggestion to my hon. friend and to members from the west generally, who pressed for many years for the building of the railway and the opening of the port. I submit that they also owe a duty to it. Considering the vast amount of money spent upon the route, and the fact that the people of eastern Canada were for many years accused of holding it up, when as a matter of fact the delay was due to war and other conditions; and considering the further fact that $50,000,000 odd has been spent upon the undertaking, I say frankly that I doubt whether western Canada itself is showing the interest it should in the problem, in the shipping of grain and other products I have been listening to a good many lectures from the west, and I respectfully submit that western Canada might listen to me in this regard. I have been listening to them a good deal. I am not saying this in any spirit of disrespect, but I do think that some of the organizations out there, which are very strong on

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
resolutions, might get to work and do more than pass resolutions; they might hunt up cargoes for Churchill. They should do a bit of the work which is not the duty of the Department of Railways or of the people of Canada as a whole.

We are all broke
up there now, and need help to get this new port started.
Have requests been made to the big grain companies of the west to furnish a cargo this year?

Yes; requests have been forwarded to the big grain companies, the pools, boards of trade and so forth. I have here a lengthy list of those to whom we sent such requests, and, I have seen a few of the answers. I may say that they were not enthusiastic. Last year I pleaded with the people of the west to ship grain through the port because I felt that it would be a black eye not only to Churchill, but a political black eye to us, if we did not get something through the port then.
I think so too.

My hon. friend is better
at painting out that it would have been a political black eye to us than he is at giving us credit for what we did do. Last year, I may say, I spoke to one big grain merchant- I will not mention his name. I had a com-versation with him in the lobby and asked him whether he would send any grain. He replied, "No, I will not send grain through Churchill. If you give me five or six cents better than the Montreal route offers I will ship through that port."
That is the point.

Otherwise, he said, he
would not consider it at all. And as a matter of fact he did not have anything to do with it. This year, as I have said, we sent letters to the boards of trade, and, frankly, we have not had satisfactory replies, but only pious wishes.

Why does
not the minister communicate with the On-To-The-Bay Association?
They have been communicating with me.
Won't they find you cargoes?

Without intending any
disrespect to the association, I may say that I was really thinking of them when I said

that if certain organizations would stop passing resolutions and hunt up cargoes instead we might make some headway.

They used
to be active in our day.
The association is still very active, but frankly, it does not supply us with cargoes. I should be glad to have their activities take that form.
I agree with the minister.

What advantage, in so
many cents, or fractions of a cent per bushel, did those cargoes have last year shipped through the bay over cargoes from Montreal?

I cannot remember exactly, [DOT]but it was in the neighbourhood of two cents. Two cents a bushel is quite a difference, and that difference was so great that Mr. McFarland came back to us and proposed that he should pay some of the charges we had not asked him to pay. He felt that he had done so well that he could pay some of the charges we had expected to pay.

Will the government be
prepared to make the same concessions this year?

I do not know that there is any necessity to make concessions, because there will be no difficulty at all in getting ships on the same basis. I do not think there will be any difficulty in getting rates out of Churchill that will be perhaps a little better than the rates of last year.
Have any negotiations been carried on with regard to the transportation of coarse grains to the maritime provinces via Hudson bay?
I have heard nothing of that suggestion, but we will be open to hear all proposals of that kind, coming either from the maritimes or from the west.

The reason I asked was because I might not be allowed to ask that question when the agriculture estimates are up. I have some memory of a statement by the Minister of Agriculture that it was hoped that large quantities of coarse grain could be shipped to the maritime provinces through Churchill for the feeding of cattle on their way to Europe. I wanted to know if that had been considered by the government.

If the Minister of Agriculture expressed that hope I have no doubt the hope was in his mind, and if it will please my hon. friend I will hope so too.

Supply-Canals-Welland
Are there still aviators investigating the course of Hudson strait?

No, there are no aviators up there now, but the vessels were so successful last year in coming in and going out that we anticipate no difficulty. We have direction finding stations there in excellent shape, and I would be a little afraid to quote the very complimentary remarks of some of the captains in comparing Churchill with some other ports. So I do not think there will be any difficulty in that regard.
Can the minister tell us about what time the straits were frozen last year?

I am afraid I cannot give that information offhand, but they are open roughly from the middle of July to the middle of October. Last year I think they were open later in the fall, because the season was very mild.
Has there been any proposal to stock Hudson bay with fish from Nova Scotia?
Has any action been taken on the resolutions which have been forwarded by various boards of trade in the west in connection with freight rates to Churchill?
Yes, that is being dealt with at the moment by the Canadian National Railways, and we expect to have them publish rates in the very near future which I hope will be very satisfactory.

I think if we have
even an average crop this year it will be pushed to the market as rapidly as possible because of the urgent need for liquidation, and I believe every exit will be required. If there is a crop like last year, however, the grain will likely go out largely via the old lines, the lines of least resistance. I would warn the government, however, that the people are in rather a distressed and complaining mood; the shoulders of the government are looked upon as broad, and the people will be apt to blame the government, whether they deserve it or not, unless that road is used to the fullest possible extent. I think the government would be well advised to get busy and not wait to be jabbed up too much by the On-to-the-Bay Association or anyone else. If there is a normal crop I do not think any difficulty will be encountered, as every avenue of egress will be used.
The government might conscript some grain.

Item agreed to.
*1761-132
Canals-Welland ship canal: construction and betterments, $3,123,400.

Could the committee
have some information on this matter?

This vote is practically
for the completion of the Welland ship canal and other supplementary works necessary at that point.

There is another
item later on in connection with this canal for $25,900.

I shall explain that item
when we reach it.

Item agreed to.
Port Colborne elevator, improvements, $1,180.
Is this elevator completed?
Yes.
How much grain went through this elevator last year?
About 30,000,000 bushels.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, April 18, 1932
